title: Array Manipulation
directAnswer: You apply m range-add operations [a, b, k] to a zero-filled array of length n, then return the maximum final value. Don't touch every cell in every range — that's O(n·m). Use a difference array: add k at index a and subtract k just past b (at b+1). One prefix-sum sweep at the end reconstructs running values; track the max as you go. Total O(n + m).

remember.pattern: Difference array + prefix sum for offline range updates
remember.formula:
diff[a] += k
diff[b + 1] -= k        # guard b+1 ≤ n
# then sweep:
running = 0; best = 0
for i in 1..n: running += diff[i]; best = max(best, running)
rules: A range-add `[a, b, k]` becomes **two** point updates: `+k` at `a`, `−k` at `b + 1` — record the boundaries, not the interior.
Use 1-based indexing and size the diff array `n + 2` so `b + 1` is always a valid index even when `b == n`.
The maximum appears **during** the prefix-sum sweep, not after — track `best` while you accumulate `running`.
Values overflow 32-bit: `k` up to 10⁹ across up to 2×10⁵ operations means use **long** in Java, plain int is fine in Python.
This works because all operations are known up front (offline) — you never need an intermediate value mid-stream.
whenToUse: Many range-add updates, then a single query (max/sum) at the end
Updates are known in advance (offline), order doesn't matter for the final array
You'd otherwise loop over each range and re-touch overlapping cells
antiSignals: Queries interleaved with updates and you need values mid-stream → Fenwick/BIT or segment tree with lazy propagation
Range updates are multiplicative or assignments, not additions → segment tree with lazy
You need every element's final value individually, not an aggregate → still fine, just do the full sweep
remember.takeaway: A range-add on an array is the derivative trick: store the *change* at the boundaries (`+k` at start, `−k` after end), then integrate once with a prefix sum. m updates in O(m), one sweep in O(n) — O(n + m) total instead of O(n·m).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that overlapping range additions don't need per-cell updates, and can express a range op as two boundary deltas reconstructed by a prefix sum. Also whether you anticipate 64-bit overflow.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Looping a[j] += k for j in [a, b] — correct but O(n·m), times out at n = 10⁷, m = 2×10⁵. Or forgetting the b+1 guard and writing out of bounds when b == n.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Call it a difference array and explain the calculus intuition: you're storing the derivative and integrating once. Mention you never even need to materialize the full array — a single running sum tracks the max.

problemStatement: Start with a 1-indexed array of `n` zeros. You're given `m` operations; each is a triple `[a, b, k]` meaning *add `k` to every element from index `a` to index `b` inclusive*. After performing all `m` operations, return the **maximum value** in the array.
understanding: You apply m additive updates to ranges of a big zero array and only care about the single largest final value. Because all updates are known ahead of time and order is irrelevant for the final state, you can defer the work: record each range as a +k/−k delta pair, then sweep once to find the peak.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are indices 1-based?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes for the classic problem. Size the diff array n+2 so b+1 is valid when b equals n.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need every final value or just the maximum?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just the maximum. That lets you track a running sum and never store the full array.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the values overflow 32 bits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. With k up to 10⁹ and many overlapping ranges, the peak can exceed 2³¹. Use a 64-bit accumulator in Java.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are operations applied in order or can I reorder them?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Addition is commutative, so order doesn't affect the final array — that's exactly why the offline difference-array trick is valid.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Apply Every Operation Cell by Cell
approaches.whenToMention: Open with it to define the problem precisely, then immediately flag the O(n·m) cost as the reason to switch.
hints: The literal reading: for each operation, walk every index from a to b and add k. What's the worst-case total work?
With n up to 10⁷ and m up to 2×10⁵, a single operation can touch the whole array. How many cell writes is that across all operations?
You re-touch overlapping cells repeatedly. Is there a way to record an operation in constant time and reconstruct values later?
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each operation can span the entire array (b − a + 1 up to n), and there are m operations: up to n·m ≈ 2×10¹² writes. Far too slow.
approaches.explanation:
Allocate the zero array and, for every operation, add `k` to each element in `[a, b]` directly.

**Why it's the obvious first move.** The problem statement literally says 'add k to every element from a to b'. Translating that word-for-word gives a double loop: outer over operations, inner over the range. It's correct and easy to reason about.

**Why it collapses at scale.** A single operation with `a = 1, b = n` writes `n` cells. With `m` such operations you do `n·m` writes — for the given limits that's around two trillion. Even at a billion simple operations per second, that's minutes, not milliseconds. The waste is *overlap*: cells covered by many ranges get rewritten over and over.

**The realization that unlocks the optimal.** We don't need the value of every cell *while* we work — only the final maximum. That means we can record each operation cheaply and reconstruct values in a single pass at the end. That reconstruction is the difference array.
approaches.insight: The brute force re-touches overlapping cells. The fix isn't a faster loop — it's recording each range as a boundary event so overlaps cost nothing extra.

approaches.name: Difference Array + Prefix Sum (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Frame it as 'store the change at the boundaries, integrate once'.
hints: Instead of marking every cell a range covers, can you mark just where the range's effect *begins* and where it *ends*?
Add k at index a (effect starts) and subtract k at index b+1 (effect ends). What operation turns these boundary marks back into actual values?
A prefix sum over the boundary marks reconstructs each cell's value. Track the maximum during that single sweep.
approaches.complexityReasoning: m operations × O(1) per boundary update = O(m). One prefix-sum sweep over n+1 entries = O(n). Total O(n + m), with O(n) space for the diff array.
approaches.explanation:
Keep a `diff` array where `diff[i]` stores the *change* in value entering index `i` rather than the value itself. A range-add `[a, b, k]` is recorded as just two edits, then a single prefix sum turns differences back into values.

**Why two edits capture a whole range.** Think of the value array as a function and `diff` as its derivative. Adding `k` across `[a, b]` is a step up of `k` at `a` and a step back down of `k` immediately after `b`. So we set `diff[a] += k` and `diff[b + 1] -= k`. The interior of the range needs no edits — once you integrate (prefix-sum), every index from `a` through `b` inherits the `+k`, and at `b + 1` the `−k` cancels it. That's why each operation is O(1) regardless of how wide its range is.

**Why the b+1 guard and size n+2.** When `b == n`, the index `b + 1 == n + 1` must exist so the subtraction doesn't crash or, worse, silently wrap. Sizing the array `n + 2` (1-based) guarantees `diff[b + 1]` is always a legal slot; we simply ignore that extra cell during the final scan.

**Why the max appears during the sweep.** Reconstructing values means `value[i] = diff[1] + diff[2] + … + diff[i]` — a running prefix sum. The peak can occur at any index, so we compare against `best` *as we accumulate*, never needing to store the full value array. This is also why we only need O(1) beyond the diff array to find the answer.

**Why 64-bit matters.** Up to 2×10⁵ overlapping operations each adding as much as 10⁹ can push the running sum past 2³¹. In Java the accumulator and diff entries must be `long`; Python integers are arbitrary precision, so no special handling.
approaches.insight: Range-add then query is the discrete analog of integrate-the-derivative. Storing changes at boundaries makes each update O(1) no matter how wide the range; one integration pass recovers everything. This same pattern powers 2D versions (image integral / submatrix sums) and interval-booking problems.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Per-cell range application
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Adding k to every cell of every range is O(n·m); at the given limits it's ~2×10¹² operations and times out.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the b+1 boundary slot
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When b == n, diff[b+1] is index n+1; an array of size n+1 has no such slot and throws.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
long[] diff = new long[n + 1];
// diff[b + 1] -= k;  // throws when b == n
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
long[] diff = new long[n + 2];
diff[b + 1] -= k;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Up to 2×10⁵ additions of 10⁹ can exceed 2³¹; the running max wraps to a wrong, often negative, value.

followupVariations.hint: If queries interleave with updates, a Fenwick tree or segment tree with lazy propagation replaces the offline diff array.

patternNote: Difference array (the discrete derivative). Record each range-add as +k at the start and −k just past the end, then integrate with one prefix-sum sweep. Turns O(n·m) range updates into O(n + m). Generalizes to 2D submatrix updates and underpins interval-booking sweeps.
